How to Play Wingspan: Rules in 20 Minutes

2026-10-21

How to play Wingspan: on your turn you either play a bird or activate one of three rows on your player mat. The forest row gets you food. The grassland row gets you eggs. The wetland row gets you cards. Stack birds into a row and that row's action gets stronger, because every bird you add upgrades the slot in front of it. After four rounds, the most points wins. You can teach the whole thing in about 20 minutes.

Then you play your first real game and lose by 30 points without seeing where they went. I did that six times, against the same friend, losing by a wider margin each night. The rules were never the problem. The rulebook is also not going to tell you where those 30 points went, because the answer is not a rule. It is timing.

I have played Wingspan more than 60 times, on a shelf that also holds three of its expansions. My worst complete game was a 52. My best is an 89. Almost all of that gap came from one change, and it had nothing to do with which birds I picked.

What Is in the Box

The 2019 box from Stonemaier Games holds 170 bird cards, 26 bonus cards, 75 egg miniatures, 40 wooden action cubes, five custom food dice, 103 food tokens, eight goal tiles, a goal board, a scorepad, and five player mats. The dice live in a cardboard birdfeeder that you tip over every time you gain food.

Every bird card is unique, hand-illustrated, and based on a real species. Printings since late 2019 also include a swift-start pack: 10 extra cards and four guides that walk you through your first four turns while you learn. Those guides are the fastest way to teach a table that has never played.

The player mat is where the game actually lives, so look at it before you read a single rule. You get three rows: forest, grassland, and wetland. Each row holds up to five birds. The left end of each row is the action, and the slots get better as you move right.

Setup in Five Minutes

Everyone takes a mat, eight action cubes, five food tokens (one of each type), two bonus cards, and five bird cards. The birdfeeder gets all five dice tossed into it.

Then comes the trade the rulebook buries in a sidebar. For every bird card you keep from your opening hand, you must discard one food token. Keep five birds and you start with zero food. Keep zero birds and you start with five food and nothing to spend it on.

Most first games go wrong right here. New players keep all five, because cards feel like the prize. Two or three is the sweet spot, and the smartest version of it is a loop: keep the bird, keep the food that bird eats. Keep a seed-eater and hold your seed token.

You also keep one of your two bonus cards, and you choose which side of the goal board to use. Here is the hidden door: the green side scores 1st, 2nd, and 3rd place for each goal, and it is the loudest part of the game. The blue side pays 1 point per targeted item up to 5, and the rulebook itself says it is the right side for new players. Take blue for your first three games. Green is where experienced players start elbowing each other.

Your Turn: Four Actions, One Cube

On your turn you place one action cube and do one of four things. Turns are short, and there is no upkeep to track.

Play a bird. Pay its food cost, plus an egg cost if it lands in the second or third slot of a row (one egg) or the fourth or fifth slot (two eggs). Then read the power printed in white: that is the "when played" power, and it only happens once, right now. Playing a bird is the only action that does not activate a row, and it is the only time you can swap food: any 2 food tokens count as any 1 food token you are missing. That trade is not legal on any other turn, so hold spare food for a bird you actually want.

Gain food. Put your cube in the forest row. The slot tells you how many dice to take out of the birdfeeder. The five dice show five food types: invertebrate, seed, fish, fruit, and rodent. One die means one token, and the wild face lets you take any of the five. Pull your dice one at a time, because taking a die can leave the tray showing five of a kind, and five of a kind is a free reroll of all five before you take anything.

Lay eggs. Put your cube in the grassland row and add that many eggs to your birds, up to each bird's printed egg limit. Extra capacity is simply lost, so spread eggs across birds with room.

Draw cards. Put your cube in the wetland row and take cards from the three-card tray or from the top of the deck.

Then slide your cube from right to left. Every brown "when activated" bird in that row fires as the cube passes it. Pink birds fire once between other players' turns. Every power is optional, and skipping one is often the correct play.

The Rows Are the Engine, Not the Birds

Here is the key insight, and it explains why a bird you could not care less about is worth a slot: your cube always lands on the first open slot in the row, so the more birds you stack, the further right your cube sits, and the slot's number is the size of the action. An empty forest row rolls one die. Two birds in that row push your cube to the third slot, and one forest action rolls three dice at once.

So a plain bird with no power is not a dead card. It is a permanent upgrade to everything sitting behind it. That is the whole engine-building idea, and once you see it, the game stops being about collecting pretty cards.

Eggs Are Money and Points at the Same Time

Eggs are the strangest part of Wingspan, and the part beginners undervalue. They cost nothing but an action. They are worth 1 point each at the end. And they are the toll you pay to play birds in the back half of every row.

Pay attention to this number: 1. Every egg on your mat is 1 point at the end of the game, and it is also one unit of currency toward your next bird. No other resource in the game pays you twice. A bird card is worth 3 to 7 points, and it costs you food, an egg or two, and a turn. An egg costs a turn and nothing else. Laying eggs is not a wasted turn. It is one of the highest-value moves on the board, and it does not look like it.

The End of a Round, and How You Score

A round ends when everyone has used all their cubes. Then four things happen in order. Everyone takes their cubes back. The end-of-round goal is scored. The three face-up tray cards are discarded and replaced. The first-player token passes left.

Scoring the goal is the competitive part. Everyone counts the targeted thing: birds in the forest, eggs on wetland birds, birds with a bowl nest, whatever the tile says. On green, first place collects the most points and ties split the total and round down. You must have at least one of the item to score anything at all. On blue, you take 1 point per item, capped at 5.

If the whole game ends in a tie, the player holding the most unused food tokens wins. It is the strangest tiebreaker in my collection, and it is the reason I never spend my last spare food on a bird I am not sure about.

There is something quiet in that step that took me a while to notice. Marking your score uses one of your action cubes. That is the real reason you get 8 turns in round 1, 7 in round 2, 6 in round 3, and 5 in round 4. The game is not shortening your turn to be cruel. It is charging you for the scoreboard.

This Is Where It Gets Interesting

For my first 20 games I built food engines. Three birds in the forest, four or five dice a turn, a pile of tokens by my mat. It felt unstoppable, and it lost constantly.

Here is the contradiction. Every guide tells you to build your engine early, and every engine quietly dies in the last two rounds. Round 4 gives you five actions in total. If two of them go to playing birds, you have three turns left to score, and any bird you play in round 4 never fires a brown power, because it arrives after the last time you will activate that row.

Then I started timing my rounds instead of building. My rule now: after round 2, stop adding birds unless the bird pays for itself in points or in eggs, and spend round 4 laying eggs and cashing in cached food. My scores moved from the low 60s into the high 70s with the same birds, the same bonus cards, and worse food. Same table, same friend. Different last two rounds.

This is also the one place where the complaints about Wingspan are fair. Reviewers have called the final round one-note, because the strongest move is usually the least interesting one. Ten games in, that is true. It is the price of a game where every point is traceable to a decision you made three rounds earlier.

Three Habits That Turn Losses Around

None of these need a spreadsheet. They need one game of paying attention.

Read the tray before you read your hand. The three face-up cards only get replaced at the end of a round. If a bird you need is sitting there, take it before the player on your left does. Denial is free, and the tray is the only shared pile in the game.

Starve the round, not the row. Do not start a fourth row of birds in round 3. Two strong rows beat three half-built ones, because a row's action scales with its own length, not your total birds.

Count eggs last, play eggs first. Look at the egg limits on your birds before you pick where eggs go. A bird with four egg slots is a scoring tile that also happens to be a bird.

Two Players, and Playing Solo

Wingspan works at any count from 1 to 5, and each count changes what the game is. Solo runs against the Automa, a small deck that plays a fake opponent and scores through end-of-round goals. It is a real opponent and not a padded one, which is why the game shows up on my solo board games list.

At two players the tray runs thin and every card denial lands twice as hard. If your group is usually two, read the Asia section below before you buy anything. The base box plays fine at two. Asia is better at two.

Which Wingspan Should You Buy

So now you know the rules. The next question is which box, because Wingspan is a small shelf of boxes now and they are not equally good at everything. Prices below are what I saw the week I checked, and they move with every sale.

Start with the base Wingspan. It was $55 on Amazon the week I checked, against a $65 list price, and it seats 1 to 5. That is the version every rule in this article refers to. Full stats live on my Wingspan page.

One honest warning. Four players is the sweet spot and five is a slog. With five, round 4 turns into a long counting exercise while the table waits for everyone to tally eggs. Two players is fast, but the card tray empties before your next turn.

The European Expansion is the first one I would add, around $30. It brings 81 new bird cards, five bonus cards, five goal tiles, and a batch of powers that trigger at the end of each round, which gives the last round something to do besides lay eggs. It also pushed my group to talk to each other more, since several of the new birds reward watching other mats.

One honest warning. Round-end powers slow the table down for the first few games. Everyone re-reads the same card twice before scoring, and rounds get noticeably longer until the group learns the batch.

Oceania, usually $32 to $35, is the one heavy players tell you to buy first, and they have a case. It adds nectar, a sixth food that works as a wild, plus five new player mats and a new set of dice. Nectar turns the early rounds loose in a way the base game never does, and the new mats make the forest row worth building past two birds. Oceania also rebalances the board on purpose: the forest and the wetland get stronger while the grassland egg engine gets weaker, and none of its new round goals reward eggs. If your table is tired of every game ending in an egg rush, this is the fix.

One honest warning. Nectar is generous, and some tables find that it flattens the first two rounds. It also went out of stock twice while I was writing this, so check the price rather than assuming the $32 I saw.

Wingspan Asia is the smart buy for two players, and it is the most interesting box in the line. It has 90 new bird cards, 14 bonus cards, and two double-sided boards, and it works three ways: as a stand-alone two-player game with a whole duet map and its own goal tiles, as a plain card expansion for the base box, and as Flock mode for 6 or 7 players. It ran $44.99 on Amazon and $39 direct from Stonemaier when I checked.

One honest warning. Duet mode is a second ruleset, not a variation. It teaches in 15 minutes, but do not hand it to a table that has never played the base game. Flock mode also needs the base game's wooden pieces, so it is not a stand-alone 7-player game.

Americas is the newest expansion, out since January 2026, and it is the one I bought on sight. It adds 111 bird cards plus 40 smaller hummingbird cards, a garden board, player mat overlays, and a hummingbird track that gives you a reason to play the little cards. About $30, and it carries a 4.9 star average on Amazon from over 100 ratings, which is about as much agreement as this hobby ever produces.

One honest warning. Those 40 hummingbird cards are mini cards, smaller than the standard bird cards, so standard sleeves will not fit them and they sit loose in the tray without the included insert. My player mat overlays also slid around until I stopped moving my mat mid-round.

Wingspan Pocket is not an expansion, and its birds do not mix with the base game. It is a stand-alone small box with 106 double-sided cards, powers printed as icons instead of sentences, and 25 to 35 minute games. It listed at $20 and I have seen it at $16 from online retailers. This is the box that goes in a bag. Stats are on my Wingspan Pocket page.

One honest warning. The icons are only obvious after you have played the base game once. Teach Pocket second, not first, or the table spends the whole game in the rulebook.

Skip the Nesting Box until you own three expansions. It costs $69 to $75 and it is a storage solution, not a game.

The Shelf Test

Here is the Shelf Test. Would this game survive 10 plays on a shelf that already holds 40 boxes? Wingspan passes that test more easily than anything else I own, and it passes for a specific reason: the rules stop being the game after night one. Ten plays in, you are not asking what a slot does. You are asking which round you should stop building, and that question never gets old.

Oceania earns the space next to it for the nectar and the sharper solo game. Asia earns it if your table is two people. The rest are luxuries.

Here is the part that matters. Get the base Wingspan first, around $55, and play your first game knowing that the last two rounds are the game. Under $50 is a good price and it does hit that on sale. If your game nights are two people, put the base box back and get Wingspan Asia instead, then add the base later if you want the flock mode for 6 or 7 players. If you are still choosing a first modern board game, my beginner list starts where this article ends, and the full strategy lineup covers what to buy after Wingspan stops surprising you.
